comment *"Multiple consumers query for a `reorder_point` column that does NOT exist on the underlying
table"*, aliasing `min_qty` as it. This consumer never moved over.

So the read has always returned 400. `supabase-js` resolves that, `status === 'fulfilled'` is true,
`data || []` gives an empty array, and the supervisor's worker drawer has always rendered **"No low-stock
items assigned"** — a statement about a person's shelf, made on a read that never once succeeded.

**The same file warns about this exact trap, eight lines above.** Its comment on the open-jobs count reads:
*"A head:true COUNT resolves with {count:null, error} rather than rejecting, so 'fulfilled' does not mean it
worked — `count || 0` reported 'Open jobs 0' for a worker whose jobs simply could not be read."* Then the
next two lines do precisely that for the logbook list and the stock list. Knowing the rule and applying it
to one of three readers is how this survives.

All three now distinguish a failed read from an empty one, and the stock read moved to the canonical view —
filtering on its `is_low_stock` flag rather than re-deriving the threshold by hand. That mattered on its
own: the hand-rolled test was `qty <= reorder_point`, which counts an item with **no threshold set** as low
the moment it reaches zero, a different rule from the one the inventory page shows for the same shelf. The
platform's inventory doctrine says it plainly — one canonical source, and the UI must not re-derive the
flags the view already computes.

The gate now asks both directions: **232 reads and writes read, 386 skipped and counted, 0 findings**,
with thirteen cases pinning what it must catch and what it must refuse to guess.

### Four functions were called unanswerable while spelling out what they wanted

The function-contract prober already knew that a complaint listing what a function accepts is an answer,
not a refusal — it reads `Available: asset, kpi` and quoted options after "must be". It did not know the two
commonest shapes on this platform:

    Missing or invalid level (must be one of day, week, month)     - one of, UNQUOTED
    Unknown section. Use parts, training, or jobs.                 - "Use", not a trigger word at all

So `level`, `source`, `table` and `section` were each reported unanswerable while the function was naming
its own vocabulary in the reply. The reader now takes an offered list in any of those shapes, strips the
quoting and trailing punctuation, and still prefers a reading verb over a writing one — six complaints,
including the original `"recall" or "store"`, all resolved to a value the function itself offered. Pinned in
the prober's self-test, and queued for a re-ask: this session's run had already started under the old
reader, so those rows still carry its verdict.

### The substrate could not describe the tables the gate most needed

The new column gate reads its schema from `substrate/table-rls/*.md`. Those notes cover **tenant tables
only** — by design, they were built to answer an RLS question, so the generator selected tables carrying
`hive_id` or `auth_uid`. That left **19 relations the pages really use with no note at all**, `hives` among
them, along with the marketplace's reviews, saved searches, watchlist, disputes and the platform-admin
table. Every read and write to those was skipped.

**The obvious fix was to parse the migrations, and measuring it first is what stopped me shipping it.**
Migrations describe every table and need no database, so `CREATE TABLE` looked like a free supplement.
Checked against the 120 tables both sources describe, the parser **misses a real column on 26 of them, 155
columns in all** — it does not follow every `ALTER` shape and cannot see a later rename. A source that wrong
would manufacture findings on exactly the tables it was added to cover, which is the failure this gate
exists to prevent. It is not used as a column authority; the tables it can name are reported as **not
known**, so the blind spot is a printed number rather than silence.

The real fix is upstream and is one line of scope: the generator now emits a note for **every base table**,
not only the tenant ones, with the heading saying which kind it is rather than calling a platform table a
tenant one. Checked before changing it, because the substrate is a shared layer: the DB-adoption census
re-filters on each note's own `has hive_id` / `has auth_uid` line, so platform tables cannot enter its
D1–D3 denominators, and the freshness gate anchors per chunk rather than by count. Queued, because it reads
the live database.

**And a latent hazard in the same source, closed while I was there.** The notes print at most fifty
columns. Nothing is truncated today — the widest table is 31 — but a table crossing that line would have
made every column past the fiftieth read as unknown, the gate manufacturing findings out of its own
source's limit. A list sitting exactly at the cap is no longer treated as a complete one.

### The teeth sweep: how many of the platform's own locks are ever pulled

_(The headline number in this section was an early count and is superseded by the corrected 1,287
below — kept because the sweep's other measurements stand, and because the way the number moved is
the point.)_

Asking the prover roster whether its own teeth are ever used:

| | carry it | ever run with it |
|---|---|---|
| `--teeth` flag | 9 | 3 |
| a self-test | 23 | 2 |

And three provers were **not registered in the suite at all** — not in `run_platform_checks.py`, not in any
script. Two of them are named as the evidence for banked rows: `prove_domain_truth` for **73** and
`prove_reward_explained` for **8**, across thirteen page banks. **A claim whose instrument nothing re-runs
cannot be re-earned and cannot be caught regressing.** That is the first of the three ways a lock is hollow:
not merely unrun, unregistered.

**Both also only exit non-zero under `--gate`**, so registering them bare would have run them and never
bitten — the second way. They carry `--gate` now, at severity `warn` until their backlog is triaged, because
a gate that hard-fails on a known-owed family teaches people to mute it.

Fifteen self-tests are registered, each **run first** to see what it needs, because registering a browser
walk as a fast check only teaches people to skip the group. That measurement was the useful part:

- **`prove_dialogs_fit_the_floor` fails 2 of 6 when the stack answers, and skips with exit 0 when sign-in
  is unavailable.** Nothing has ever reported either. Registered so the failure is visible; whether those
  two cases are a broken oracle or a saturated host is what its next run settles.
- **`prove_flow_fits_the_floor` passed and then failed within the same hour** — its self-test drives a real
  sheet, so it is stack-dependent, not pure. Seven self-tests that touch a browser moved behind the
  fast-skip; the five that do not were each run twice and confirmed green both times before being left as
  fast checks.
- **`prove_component_states_scoped` is registered nowhere and cited by no banked row** — dead tooling. Its
  self-test is registered with that said plainly, so it is either used or retired on purpose rather than by
  drift.

**And my own instruments were wrong three times inside this one audit.** The first sweep reported "0 of 9
teeth ever run" because it matched a literal `"script": "..."` while registrations use `os.path.join`. Two
later measurements read `$?` after a pipeline and so reported the exit code of `tail`. Each time the number
was alarming and the code was fine — the same shape as every finding above, pointed the other way.

### It was 1,287 claims, and my first three counts of it were all wrong

Following the same question through the `--teeth` flags and then through every prover on disk, the number
moved three times, and each move was my instrument rather than the platform:

1. **"0 of 9 teeth ever run"** — the sweep matched a literal `"script": "..."` while registrations use
   `os.path.join`. Corrected: 3 of 9.
2. **"six provers registered nowhere, about six hundred claims"** — two were not orphans. Their ids already
   existed, pointing at Python validators of the same name; my search was for the prover *filename*.
3. **"fourteen unregistered, 2,240 claims"** — wrong the other way. A prover is not unrun because the suite
   does not name it: **a registered Python gate can drive it by subprocess**, and four of the fourteen are
   driven exactly that way — the offline queue's gate runs all eight cases *with a retry*. Being merely
   *named* in a Python file is not it either; several appear only in a docstring's "Re-drive:" line.

**The number that survives all three corrections: 1,287 banked claims rest on six provers that nothing in
this repository runs** — not the suite, not a committed script, not another gate.

| prover | banked rows citing it | what it measures |
|---|---|---|
| `prove_journey` | 446 | the 66-persona walk: first run, repeat visit, two-sided flows, abandon, hand-off |
| `prove_view_contrast` | 315 | contrast in the views a person opens, not the default one |
| `prove_availability_pages` | 242 | offline refusal, retry path, rate-limit legibility across the page set |
| `prove_safe_area` | 203 | a control under the notch is unreachable on the phone it was designed for |
| `prove_domain_truth` | 73 | is this the ISO 14224 definition of MTBF |
| `prove_reward_explained` | 8 | a reward shown without its criteria is a number, not a motivator |

`prove_journey` is the sharpest: its own header carries a lesson the whole platform later adopted (*"a fixed
filename let a one-page test DESTROY a 66-persona run"*), two other gates quote it in their labels, and
nothing ever invoked it.

All six are registered, behind the fast-skip because they need the live stack, at severity `warn` until a
first suite reading exists. Where a verdict lives behind `--gate` the registration carries that flag —
including `prove_safe_area`, whose **entire** verdict does, so my own first registration would have walked
every page, written its report and never failed. That is the second way a lock is hollow, committed by me in
the hour I finished writing about it.

**Eleven registrations were withdrawn** once the subprocess drivers were found — three duplicates and the
eight I had added per offline-queue case, which the existing gate already covers better than mine did.

**`prove_availability_pages` is registered honestly rather than usefully**: it exits non-zero on a crash,
not on findings, so its green is not a verdict. Registering it re-earns the evidence 242 rows stand on, and
the label says so, because a report-only check whose label implies judgement is the narrow-instrument fault
one more time.

### "Nothing tells a returner how old this is" — on four pages that say so

Triaging the lifecycle walk's first findings while it ran, four pages failed the returner lens. Two of them
were the instrument, one was the instrument in a subtler way, and none of the four needed a product change.

**The oracle did not know the platform's own words.** It looked for "updated", "as of", "last refreshed",
"just now", "minutes ago". Harvesting what the platform actually writes:

| freshness string | pages |
|---|---|
| `Live · refreshed on load` | 14 |
| `live` | 7 |
| `Live data` | 6 |
| `Live · updates automatically` | 4 |
| `Recalculated weekly`, `daily snapshot`, `Recomputed when this report was generated` | 1 each |

**Not one of the commonest matched.** Pages that state their freshness plainly were failing a check about
whether they state it — the same shape the domain-truth prover's header records being bitten by five times
in one arc, each time with the product right.

**And widening the word list would have been the wrong repair twice over.** "Live" appears in ordinary page
text — a live map, live updates — so accepting it would have made the check nearly vacuous. The platform
renders this claim through **one component**: `renderSourceChip` emits `<p class="wh-source-chip"
role="status">`. So the honest question is whether that chip is present and says something, with the phrase
list kept for pages that state freshness in their own prose.

**Then the first version of that fix introduced a false pass**, caught before it ran. `llm-observability`'s
chip is a placeholder reading *"Loading the cost and cache rollup"*, and a bare length test would have
credited a stuck spinner as a statement about how old the data is — trading one wrong verdict for a quieter
one. A chip counts only once it has settled into saying something.

**And that page turned out not to be a finding at all.** It fills the same chip with *"· as of 15:42 ·
refreshes on each window change"* the moment its query lands — which the original regex would have matched.
Read mid-load it carries no skeleton class and no `aria-busy`, so the walk judged a settled page and
reported a missing affordance that is right there a second later. **A text placeholder is a skeleton no
skeleton-finder sees.** A status region still announcing that it is loading now means the page has not
finished, and the verdict is unreadable rather than bad.

Three corrections, all to the instrument, on a run that is still going.

### Two more of the same, from the same run

**"A stranger sees 257 chars" on the seller profile.** That page reads its subject from `?worker=`, and
without one it renders exactly what it should: *"No seller specified. This page needs a seller name in the
URL. Open it via marketplace.html"*, with a back link. The walk arrived bare and graded a correct, legible
empty state as a failure to explain itself. **A page that needs a subject must be visited with one** — the
journey prover already does, so the lifecycle walk now uses the same fixture in the same words, and both
instruments read the same page.

**"At 768: 32 controls under 40px" on the landing page.** Every visible link counted as a tap target,
including the prose links inside sentences — and the target-size rule excepts those itself, because
enlarging a link would break the sentence it lives in. A number that large about a page nobody has
complained about is the tell. The exception is now applied exactly as written: **inline display and
embedded in text longer than the link itself**. A small button, or a link styled as one, is neither, so
nothing real is excused — verified against all four shapes.

That is five instrument corrections from one run's first fifty rows, and no product change among them. The
pattern is consistent enough to be worth stating plainly: **on a mature platform, a lens that reports many
findings at once is usually reporting itself.** The three that turned out to be real defects this session —
the moderation badge, the worker drawer's stock list, the escalation flag — each showed up as *one* row, not
thirty.

### And an invitation read as a refusal

`public-feed.html` is a public, read-only feed. Its subtitle says *"Sign in to join the conversation"* and
its call to action says *"Sign in to post"* — and the walk reported **"a stranger meets a refusal, not the
page"**, because the refusal detector matched the words "sign in" anywhere in the text.

**A refusal means the content was withheld.** The journey prover already carries the right definition for
exactly this question — a sign-in prompt near the top *and* a page too short to be showing anything else —
so it is reused rather than re-invented. A feed rendering its posts alongside a join CTA is 5,000 characters
long and passes; a bare gate is 60 and does not.

`status.html` fell to the freshness rule and is covered by the same chip fix: its chip reads **"Live ·
probes run on load"**, which the old word list did not recognise either.

That is seven instrument corrections from one run, and the run is not finished. None of the seven changed a
page. The count is worth keeping next to the three real defects this session found, because it is the
clearest evidence yet for the rule the whole programme keeps rediscovering: **the instrument is wrong far
more often than the product, and a lens reporting many findings at once is usually reporting itself.**

### A page that is not for strangers, graded by a stranger's lens

The last three findings of the run were `ph-intelligence` and `platform-actions`, each answering a search
arrival and a cold link with a few hundred characters. Both say in their own text what they are:
**"members only" / "supervisor"** and **"Founder"**. They are internal surfaces, and a stranger meeting a
short, legible explanation is the behaviour you want — not a failure to hand over the contents.

Both arrival lenses now accept a legible refusal from a page that declares itself internal, read from **the
page's own words** rather than a list kept in the prover, so a page that later opens up stops being excused
automatically. A refusal still has to be legible: under 250 characters it is a blank door, not an
explanation.

That is eight corrections from one run of one prover, every one of them to the instrument. The run is still
going, and it will be re-run from the top with all eight in place, because a verdict from a lens I have
since corrected is not evidence either way.

### The whole run was about the host, and it said so in line three

Reading the lifecycle walk's opening lines rather than only its verdicts:

    WITHOUT AN IDENTITY (the database could not name the hive this person belongs to)
      - every hive page will be the door, and those rows will report that rather than pretend

**Every one of the 202 rows was walked as nobody.** Fifty-nine correctly reported "this cell reaches the
door, not the page", and the rest were read through a lens that had no session behind it. An hour of
browser time, and none of it evidence about the platform.

**The cause is one line, and it is the session's own lesson for the fourth time.** The prover's `psql`
helper returned `''` both when a query answered nothing and when five attempts all failed. So
`if (!hive)` read an unreachable database as *"this person is in no hive"* — and the lifecycle step had
started seconds after a sixty-two-function edge sweep let go of the database. The identity read lost that
race, and a host problem became a statement about the product.

Two repairs:

- **A successful query now returns its answer whatever it is; only an unreachable database returns null**,
  so the two cases have different sentences. One is about the platform (*"is in no active hive"*), the
  other about the machine (*"did not answer after five attempts"*). The first-timer cast carried the same
  conflation and now carries the same distinction.
- **An unreadable identity stops the run before the walk.** A host problem deserves a host answer, not two
  hundred rows of non-evidence. The browser slot releases on the way out, so nothing is left holding it.

That the prover reported its own blindness honestly, in its first three lines, is why this was findable at
all — and it is also why the verdicts underneath it were never worth reading. **A run that announces it has
no identity should not then spend an hour grading pages.**

### Fifty-four percent of the companion's certified capability is never called

The four dead compliance functions were not an accident of one file. Twenty `validate_ai_companion_*.py`
validators guard `voice-handler.js`, and **every check they make asks whether a name is spelled in the
source.** Measured:

| | count |
|---|---|
| symbols those validators guard and the file defines | 283 |
| never called anywhere inside the file | 154 |
| never called **anywhere** — not the file, not a page, not a test, not a tool | **73** |

The 81 in between are reached by the Playwright sentinel through the export surface, which the file's own
header says is deliberate. Those are genuinely called. **The 73 are not called by anything.**

**Four of the 73 were opened by hand today, and all four were also wrong** — each writing to `event_type`,
a column `ai_audit_log` does not have. They had never been exercised, so the mistake kept. That is the
whole argument for counting this: **dead code is not merely absent, it is untested, and it rots in place
while a gate certifies it.**

Seventy-three is a backlog, not a session. So it is now **measured and ratcheted** rather than invisible:
a gate reports the number every run, `--list` names them, and the baseline can only fall. Three honest
fixes lower it — wire the capability to the path that should call it, move it to the layer it belongs in
and point the validator there (retention became a `pg_cron` job today), or delete it and drop its check.
Leaving it certified is not one of them.

Its own teeth pin the distinctions that make the number trustworthy: a symbol a test calls is not counted,
one reached through the export surface is not counted, and **a comment naming a symbol is not a call** —
which matters in a file that now explains its own bugs at length.

### One of the seventy-three, taken out rather than left certified

`_buildAuditCsv` and its `_toCsvRow` helper are gone. They were a second, weaker CSV writer for voice
activity — defined, exported, and called by nothing anywhere in the repository since the day they were
written, and wrong the whole time (an `event_type` header against a table whose column is `event`)
**precisely because nothing exercised them**. Removed rather than annotated: a duplicate kept "in case" is
a second thing to keep correct.

The requirement did not move, only its address. The compliance gate's audit-export check now asks
`audit-log.html` — which owns the platform's real export, with its own escaping and a byte-order mark so
Excel does not mangle an asset name — whether it still **reads** `ai_audit_log` and still **offers** the
export. If either disappears, it reddens. All twelve compliance checks pass against the new address.

A small correction to my own expectation, worth keeping: this did **not** lower the reachability baseline.
Deleting a symbol takes it out of the *guarded* set, not the *dead* set — guarded fell 283 → 281 and the
count of never-called stayed at 73. The number only falls when a capability that is still certified gets a
caller. That makes the ratchet stricter than I described it, which is the right direction.

### The two contracts the banker held, and only one of them was a defect

The function-contract sweep closed at **68 of 70 holding**, and held two findings rather than banking
around them.

**`agent-memory-store` — real, and fixed.** *"Answered 200, but its source has no catch that returns a
response — a provider failure would reach the person raw."* Its input handling is careful: a bad method, an
unreadable body, a missing `op` and a refused tenancy each get their own legible sentence. But once the work
starts, a throw from the database or the shared episodic-memory helpers left the Deno runtime to answer, and
the caller got a raw 500 with a stack in it. The recall path is the one that matters — a worker asking the
companion what it remembers should be told it could not look, not shown an exception, and above all not be
handed an empty list. It now answers 503 with *"Your memory could not be reached just now. Nothing was lost
— try again in a moment."*

**`benchmark-compute` — not a defect, and the queue already settles it.** *"The call never returned and
nothing in its source bounds it."* The bound half is true and irrelevant: that function makes **no outbound
call at all**, so there is nothing to bound; it computes against the database. What the reading actually
says is that the work took longer than the prober's 35-second budget — a statement about the probe, and the
`--patient` pass at 135 seconds is exactly the instrument for it. Banking a red here would have accused a
slow query of being an unbounded provider call.

The distinction is the same one this session kept meeting: **a bound is missing** and **I hung up first**
are different findings, and only the first is about the platform.

### The fix landed the minute it was written

The chain's last step, the tier-B language sample, produced no result file. Its log says why:

    FAIL full-journeys - the database did not answer, so the solo cast could not be read
                         (start the stack, then re-run)

That sentence did not exist an hour earlier. The solo-cast loader used to return an empty list for both
"nobody like that exists" and "I could not ask", and the run above it had just spent an hour with the
database. **Under the old code the sample would have walked tier B as nobody and banked verdicts about a
sign-in door** — the same hour of non-evidence the lifecycle walk had already produced, in the very next
step. Instead it refused, said which of the two had happened, and asked for a quiet host. It is queued to
get one.

**The chain closed at 79.8% — 3,158 of 3,959 — up from 79.3% at the start of the turn.** The movement is
small on purpose: almost everything found today was an instrument, and correcting an instrument does not
move a percentage, it decides whether the percentage means anything.

### Working the backlog: 73 to 71

Two of the uncalled capabilities were wired, each to the one place its own header says it belongs.

**The knowledge-gap log fires where the knowledge actually runs out.** Its comment promises a row in
`ai_knowledge_gap` "when the companion can't answer, so the supervisor can prioritise backfilling the truth
view", and the table has always been empty because nothing called it. The obvious trigger was the reply
text, and it is the wrong one: every offline fallback says *"I'm offline right now"*, which is a
connectivity gap, not a knowledge one, and logging those would fill a supervisor's list with the wrong
thing. The right place is the retrieval fall-through, where the system knows the truth — the hive's own
knowledge base was asked and could not answer — and the reason it names comes from the loop's own outcome:
`rag_miss` when nothing usable came back, `low_confidence` when the loop answered and its own checker
refused it. Those are the words the table's column comment already documents.

**The monthly cost cap is enforced for the first time.** `_getMonthlyCost` and `_exceededCostCap` sit under
a comment describing the exact behaviour — *"when the running total breaches the cap, the next turn is
short-circuited to a 'monthly cap reached' reply"* — and neither was called. There was also **no cap value
anywhere**: no column, no constant, no config. A comparison with nothing to compare against.

**The wiring deliberately does not pick a number.** What a hive may spend per month is a commercial
decision, and the AI chain runs on permanently-free provider tiers where a turn costs nothing, so any figure
would be invented rather than derived. The new column defaults to **0, which the existing guard already
reads as no cap at all**. Nothing changes for any hive until somebody sets one, and the moment somebody
does, the enforcement is real. It also costs nothing while unset: the spend query walks up to ten thousand
rows, so the cap is read once per session and, at 0, the whole block is one property lookup. An unreadable
setting reads as uncapped rather than capped-at-zero, because the second would mute the companion on a
failed read.

The reply says what happened rather than just refusing: the budget is the hive's own setting, it resets next
month, the question is saved, and a supervisor can raise it.

**73 → 71**, with one more removed as a dead duplicate earlier. The remaining 71 are named by
`--list`, and each is a promise the platform makes that nothing performs.

### Docker wedged, and the queue was the reason

At 16:21 the follow-up queue stopped producing output. Docker's engine was returning **500 Internal Server
Error to every call** — `docker ps`, `docker version`, everything — and zero containers were running. The
whole local stack was gone: database, auth, edge runtime.

**390 MB free of 8 GB.** That is the host pattern this project already has a name for, and the queue is what
walked into it: an hour-long lifecycle walk, a sixty-two-function edge sweep, and seven journey re-walks
lined up behind them, on a machine where the editor alone holds 1.9 GB across twenty-one processes.

Recovery, in order:

1. **Stopped the two blocked background jobs.** Both were parked on a `docker exec` that would never
   answer, and one of them would have proceeded on a false reading the moment Docker came back.
2. **Restarted the engine.** The evidence supported that specific action and no other: every API call
   failing, zero containers, and the VM squeezed to 552 MB.
3. **Waited for the database rather than assuming it.** It answered "the database system is starting up"
   first, then 22 active members ten seconds later.
4. **Started the edge runtime by hand** — it had exited 255 and did not come back with the rest. A function
   answers again.

**And then did not restart the queue.** The host still has ~320 MB free, and re-running seven browser walks
is how it wedged the first time. So the queue is split: **the half that needs no browser is running now** —
the substrate rebuild, the fleet completions and audit trail, the community answers, the two solo personas,
and the fleet alert scan. Every one of those is a **precondition** for a walk that is waiting, so doing them
under a memory ceiling means the walks are one step rather than ten when there is room.

That is the degraded-instrument rule applied to the host itself: the browser is unavailable, the database
and the edge runtime are not, and there is real work that only needs the second kind.

### What the no-browser half actually did

Every precondition the waiting walks need is now in place, and three of the four steps taught something.

**The alert census confirmed the deduction exactly.** Measured, not inferred from a `least()`: Manila 61
alerts, Lucena 40, Baguio 27, and **all three fleets zero**. That is the missing link J2 reported, read
straight from the table.

**The fleet completions failed, and the reason is a column whose name is not its meaning.**
`pm_completions.asset_id` is a foreign key to **`pm_assets`**, not to `asset_nodes` — the column named for a
machine points at the SCHEDULE ROW. The seeder joined through `asset_nodes` to get "the asset this PM is
about", which is what the name says, and every insert was refused: *"Key (asset_id)=… is not present in
table pm_assets."* The seeder reported "the completion insert did not answer" and moved on, **because psql
returns None for a refusal exactly as it does for an unreachable database** — the same conflation this
session fixed in two provers, met a third time from the writing side. Corrected to the schedule's own id,
which is also the truer reading: a completion completes a schedule. All three fleets now hold them.

**The community answers landed where they could, and said so where they could not.** Three plant hives have
six replies each, two accepted. The three fleets have **no posts at all**, so there was nothing to answer,
and the seeder reported that rather than inventing a question to answer. Two of them also have fewer than
two members, so nobody there could answer somebody else.

**Both solo personas were created and their sign-in verified** before the tool reported success. J11 and
J31 have a person to walk as, and the first-timer cast has a castable account.

**And a count that had been one too many, everywhere.** The seeder said "wrote 7 answers"; the table held
six. `psql -tA -c "insert … returning id"` prints the ids **and** its `INSERT 0 6` command tag, so counting
output lines always overshoots by one. `seed_fleet_history.py` already knew this — its own docstring records
a logbook entry once written about a van called *"INSERT 0 2"* — and the fix lived only inside that file's
`psql()`. The community seeder had the same shape and none of the fix. It now strips the tag in the same
place, so both read a result the same way.

**Three migrations applied locally and verified**: the cost-cap column with its default of 0, the escalation
unique key, and the retention cron (`pg_cron` is present and nothing is old enough to be deleted, so it
removes nothing today). **The column gate caught my own cost-cap read** before any of that, naming a column
that existed only in a migration — which is precisely the class it was built for, pointed at me.

With the substrate rebuilt past tenant tables, that gate now knows **178 tables instead of 123**, has one
unknown left instead of 56, and reads **268 sites instead of 232**. All 864 substrate chunks are fresh.

### The person between anonymous and member had nowhere to go

Driving the solo journey to its end found a real defect, and it took three corrections to see it.

**First the cast, then the chain, then the setup.** The two personas could sign in (7 of 8 steps arriving
as themselves, up from a sign-in door). Then the chain read `logbook where hive_id='$H'` — and a solo story
has **no hive**, so `$H` templated an empty string, Postgres refused the malformed statement, and the walk
reported *"the database did not answer"*. It had answered perfectly well; the question was malformed. Chains
can now be scoped to a **person** with `$W`, and both solo chains are: a one-person operator's records are
keyed to them, and a resume belongs to a worker rather than to the platform. Then the personas had no
records at all, which for a brand-new account is honestly true — so they keep their own logbook now, under
no hive, which is a shape the platform already holds in six rows.

**And the walk was stamping a hive on a person who has none.** `signInAs` wrote `wh_active_hive_id`
unconditionally, so a hive-less story got an empty hive key. Removed, because a person with no hive is
signed in as exactly that.

**Then the finding, measured in three states:**

| who | what they get |
|---|---|
| anonymous | 14,428 characters of the marketing landing |
| signed in, in a hive | the real operations home |
| **signed in, no hive** | **604 characters, and every control pointing at hive-scoped tools** |

The PM scheduler, analytics and the logbook are all offered to someone who has no hive for them to read.
**Nothing anywhere said "join a hive with a code, or start your own"** — the one thing that person needs,
and the entire premise of the journey they are cast in: no hive, grows into one.

The card at the top of the operations home exists to show **one decision**, and for this person that is the
decision. It now says so, links to the hive board, and adds the part that matters to a solo operator:
*"Your own records stay yours either way — a hive adds the people you work with."* Verified in all three
states: it appears only for the hive-less, and that page went from 604 characters to 1,207.

**What remains is a path question, not a defect.** The journey still reports three hops with no way onward,
and two of them are a public learn page and a calculator having no link to the hive board. A public article
linking into somebody's hive board is a design decision, not an omission, so the row's declared path is what
needs deciding — and that belongs in the roadmap rather than in a page.

### The funnel: from a crash, to nothing, to three of three

J12 is the public-to-member funnel — a search result, a free calculator, the sign-in, the hive board, a
first logbook entry. It began the day by **crashing the prover** on a temporal dead zone that only it could
reach. Four corrections later it holds end to end, and every one of them was the instrument.

**A conversion funnel changes who is walking it.** The walk casts one identity per story, so J12 walked as
one anonymous person and reported the hive board and the logbook bouncing to the landing page — correct for
a stranger, and silent about the funnel, whose entire point is that they stop being one. The action map
built for J13 already runs code inside a page mid-walk and the browser context persists across steps, so
the conversion is expressible as an action **at the page where a person converts**. Signing in as an
existing plain member stands in for a join-by-code the walk has no code for, and the receipt says so rather
than implying the join was exercised. The member was chosen with no platform-admin rights on purpose.

**Then the chain asked about a hive the story does not carry.** `hives where id='$H'` on a story with no
vertical is unreadable by construction. What a funnel has to be true about is the **destination**: a public
arrival is only a funnel if there is a hive on the other side, with members in it.

**Then "walked with NO identity" was reported about a story that had just signed in.** Judging a conversion
by the identity it was *cast* with reports the premise as the failure. A story whose action converted has an
identity from that page onward, and the steps prove it: three of five pages arriving became five of five.

**And the last dead hop was a link the matcher could not see.** The walk matches an onward link by
filename, and the public pages link home as `href="/"` and `href="/#join"` — which **is** the landing page.
So a free calculator that plainly invites the reader in read as "no way onward at all". My first repair was
worse than the bug: matching any href starting with a slash would have credited `/learn/` and
`/engineering-design.html` as links to the landing page, handing every page a way onward it does not have.
Tightened to the site root itself, and pinned with eleven cases.

**I nearly reported that as a product defect**, and the sweep that would have carried it was mine too: a
grep for `index.html` across the sixty calculator pages returned "0 of 60 link back to the product", when
every one of them links home as `/`. Reading one page's actual anchors is what stopped it.

### The AI-assisted day, proved by performing it

J13 now holds in **all six hives**, and the last bug took three probes to find because I had hidden it
myself.

The walk drove `WHVoice.dispatch` — the product's own public dispatcher, the same function the confirm
button calls — and the handler ran: the form pre-filled, the receipt said so. And **no audit row appeared,
and nothing said why.** The emitter worked when called directly through its export; a raw insert worked; the
live `dispatch` function demonstrably contained the call. Everything measured said it should work.

**The catch I wrote was swallowing the reason.** Made to speak, it said it in one line:

    [WHVoice] could not record the action: _s(...).slice is not a function

`_scrubPii` returns **`{ text, scrubs }`**, not a string — it reports how many it replaced, which is the
better contract and not the one its name suggests. My scrubbing helper called `.slice()` on the object, the
throw was caught, and the audit simply did not happen.

Two lessons, and the second is the one worth keeping. The first is the ordinary one: read what a function
returns, do not infer it from the name. The second is that **I wrote the empty catch in the same session I
spent criticising them** — the comment even argued for it, that an audit write must never undo the action it
records. That argument is right and it justifies catching; it does not justify catching *quietly*. Three
probes went into establishing what one `console.warn` said immediately.

The row that lands is what the header always promised: `logbook.create`, the worker, and the intent and
outcome with PII scrubbed. The walk counts it, then deletes it — **zero rows left behind, the table back to
empty** — so the evidence is produced and returned rather than accumulated.

### Two instruments disagreed about the same hop, and the static one was wrong

The live walk said three of J11's hops had no way onward. The path gate said **zero hops follow no route**,
across all 39 archetypes. One of them was wrong about the same pages.

**The gate credited a hub that is not on the page.** It reads `nav-hub.js` for what the hub offers, then
treats any hop as reachable if the hub offers the destination — without asking whether the page the person
is *standing on* carries the hub. Measured: **32 of 42 root pages load it, and zero of the learn articles
and calculators do** — the entire public funnel. So the gate was answering a question about the hub while
the walk was answering one about a page.

Taught to ask, it went from 0 broken hops to 6 — agreeing with the walk about J11 and finding five more.

**Then it over-reported one, for the same reason the walk had.** Its link reader stripped slashes from an
href, so `href="/"` became the empty string and was dropped for not ending in `.html`. Every public page
links home that way. Both instruments now read a root link as the landing page, and they agree: 5 broken
hops, each with a route.

**And the repair tool crashed on the line that reports what it could not fix.** `where` is a list of
candidate routes and the line concatenated it to a string — a reporting line that fails exactly when there
is something to report. It had never run, because until the gate learned about the hub there was never any
residue.

**What the repair then surfaced is a product finding, not a path detail.** Three destinations are reachable
only by going back to the home page first:

| destination | wanted by |
|---|---|
| `project-manager.html` | 2 hops |
| `community.html` | 1 hop |
| `skillmatrix.html` | 1 hop |

The tool's own words for it are the right ones: *"the person must go home to get there."* Applying the
repair would route the journeys through the landing page and grow one archetype from 5 pages to 13, which
changes what those rows measure — so the repair is left as a deliberate step, and the finding is recorded
as what it is: three surfaces with no route into them except the front door.

### The repair was applied, did not converge, and was reverted

With the gate honest, the repair tool had work to do, so it was run: 25 rows across four archetypes, and
the broken hops fell from 5 to 2. Run again, it wrote nine more rows and the **same two hops persisted** —
the gate suggesting `asset-hub.html` one pass and `logbook.html` the next, the tool inserting each in turn.

**J11 grew from 8 pages to 16 and was no better.** That is not a repair; it is a loop with a page count
attached. Reverted from the backup taken before the first apply, which is why one was taken.

What survives is what was earned separately: **J31's single-hop correction stands** — routing the portfolio
through `skillmatrix.html`, which is where the platform parents achievements — because that route was
unambiguous and it took the walk from 0 of 2 to 2 of 2.

The gate stays red on **2 hops**, and that is the honest state. It was green before today only because it
credited a nav hub that is not on the page. A red gate naming `learn/index.html → hive.html` and
`platform-actions.html → hive.html` is worth more than a green one that never asked.

**And the residue is a product finding rather than a path detail**: `analytics.html` and `community.html`
are reachable only by going back to the landing page first. Two significant surfaces with no route into
them except the front door.

### The 1,287 was wrong, and the suite's own check is what caught me

**Correction, and it is the largest of the session.** The claim that 1,287 banked rows cite provers nothing
runs was false for five of the six. `tools/validate_page_ui_provers.py` drives **nineteen provers from a
lookup table**, registered under **21 gate ids** — including `prove_journey` (446 rows), `prove_view_contrast`
(315), `prove_safe_area` (203), `prove_domain_truth` (73) and `prove_reward_explained` (8). They run.

**Four separate detectors of mine missed it**, each for a different reason, and the reason matters: that
runner *builds* the filename from a table and executes `node <probe>`, so every pattern that looked for the
prover's name inside a `subprocess.run([...])` call found nothing. A fifth read of the table only saw three
entries because I sliced twenty lines out of the middle of it.

**What actually caught the mistake was the platform, not me.** Running the static board with my
registrations in place, the suite refused to start:

    REGISTRY ERROR — a report artifact is claimed by more than one gate:
      domain_truth_report.json <- domain-truth, ci_domain_truth
      journey_report.json <- journey-personas, cn_journey
      reward_explained_report.json <- reward-explained, cm_reward_explained

Three collisions, each naming the existing gate I had duplicated. **The check that found my error is the
kind of check this whole session has been about**, and it did in one line what five of my sweeps could not.

**Then I made it worse before making it better.** Removing the five duplicates with a regex deleted **443
registrations** — the runner went from 1,230 checks to 787. Restored from git and re-applied deliberately by
appending complete entries at the list's end rather than pattern-matching through it. Verified by loading
the module and asking it: 1,111 checks, no duplicate ids, no missing scripts, **no report artifact claimed
twice**.

**What survives of the finding:**

- `prove_availability_pages` — **242 banked rows, and genuinely run by nothing.** The only file naming it
  reads its report and is itself unregistered. Registered, at severity `warn`, with its report-only nature
  stated so its green is not read as a verdict.
- **The teeth half stands and is untouched by the correction.** That runner drives nineteen walks with
  `--gate` and **never a self-test**, so a prover's own teeth are unrun even where its walk is not. Ten are
  registered, each run first to see whether it needs the live stack.

The lesson is the session's own, turned on its author: **a sweep that reports something alarming is
reporting itself until proven otherwise**, and the proof is reading the one file it names rather than
writing a sixth pattern.

### The proof that the earlier run was about the host

Re-run on a quiet stack, the lifecycle walk opens with three lines it could not produce before:

    walking 202 cell/lifecycle/layer row(s)
      and a first-timer: consumer.walk@workhive.test - an account with no hive and no history
      signed in as Wilfredo Malabanan - these are the pages, not the door

**The first-timer it found is an account that was there all along.** `consumer.walk@workhive.test` has no
hive and no history, which is exactly what the new-user cells need, and the earlier run reported *"the
database holds no account without a hive, so a first-timer cannot be cast."* That sentence was never true.
It was the helper returning the same empty string for "nobody like that exists" and "five attempts all
failed", on a host that had just finished a sixty-two-function edge sweep.

So the fix is confirmed by the thing it fixed: the same query, the same database, a quiet moment, and the
account appears. Every one of the previous run's 202 verdicts was about the machine, and the ten solo
personas and portfolios seeded since were not what unblocked it. They are still right to exist, and the
run that follows this one is the first that measures the platform.


## W3-JN finding · `offline-3g` closes at HALF the rate of every other condition (measured 2026-09-10)

The condition axis was seeded four ways, twenty rows each. Their closure rates are not comparable:

| condition | rows | closed | still open |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| normal | 664 | **83%** | 111 |
| dependency-down | 20 | **75%** | 5 |
| release-mid-way | 20 | **75%** | 5 |
| **offline-3g** | **20** | **40%** | **12** |

Half the closure rate of the other two adverse conditions is a pattern, not a run of bad luck, and the two
rows read in detail fail the same way:

- **W3654** (J4, audit season, Ramos Jeepney Line) — 7 of 8 pages rendered 500-2,000 characters; `hive.html`
  rendered nothing. The prover re-asked in a fresh browser on its own and it failed identically, which is
  what separates a defect from a load artifact on this program.
- **W3512** (J1, onboarding, Manila Electronics Assembly) — every hop after `hive.html` reported no route
  onward at all, while the same archetype's other 37 rows walked.

**THE MECHANISM, and it is the honest reason these are harder than the other conditions.** The emulation
aborts one request in twelve (`prove_full_journeys.mjs`: `if (++n % 12 === 0) route.abort('connectionfailed')`)
AND the walk unregisters the service worker on every context (`navigator.serviceWorker.getRegistrations()
.then(rs => rs.forEach(r => r.unregister()))`). That combination is not a contrived worst case — it is
exactly a **FIRST-TIME VISITOR on a lossy Philippine connection**: no cache primed, nothing precached, and
a one-in-twelve chance that any given shell asset simply never arrives. A returning installed user is
protected by `sw.js`; a first visit is not, and there is no inline fallback when `nav-hub.js` is the
request that gets dropped — the navigation is simply absent.

It is also why the arithmetic bites hardest on the biggest page: at a 1-in-12 drop rate, a page making
twenty reads loses one far more often than a page making two, and `hive.html` is the platform's largest
board. So the question these rows really ask is not *whether* a read drops but **whether the page says so
or shows nothing**, and the walks say nothing.

**NEXT (needs a quiet host - two Playwright jobs, or a browser walk beside the 500-check suite, is what
crashed J25 and J19 today):**

1. Walk `hive.html` alone under the same emulation and watch a dropped read: a legible "couldn't load"
   with a retry is the product working; a permanent skeleton or an empty board is the defect. That
   distinction is invisible to every static gate.
2. If it is the defect, the fix is not per-page: a dropped SHELL asset needs a retry or a minimal inline
   nav fallback, so a first visit on a bad line still has a way onward. `whQueryTimeout` is adopted on
   exactly one page (marketplace.html, 3 sites) - the other pages in these chains have none.
3. Re-walk the 12 open `offline-3g` rows after that, and expect the rate to move as a group. If it does
   not, the condition is measuring the emulator rather than the platform, and the emulator is the thing
   to correct.

## W3-JN finding · the Supabase client is a THIRD-PARTY CDN fetch the service worker can never cache (2026-09-10)

Three findings I had been filing separately turn out to share one cause, and it is visible in four greps.

**The dependency.** 37 pages load the client that does all auth and all data access from
`https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@supabase/supabase-js@2.110.0/dist/umd/supabase.min.js`. Nothing on this
platform works without it.

**It can never enter the cache.** `SHELL_FILES` holds no cross-origin entry at all (checked by parsing the
array, not by grepping the bump prose - `supabase-js precached: False`). And the cache-on-visit path added
on 2026-09-09 is explicitly same-origin:

    const _keepable = _req.method === 'GET'
      && new URL(url).origin === self.location.origin        // <- jsdelivr can never qualify
      && /\/(learn|tools)\//.test(new URL(url).pathname);

So the one script the whole platform depends on is fetched fresh from a third party on every visit,
precached by nothing, cached-on-visit by nothing, and guarded by no `onerror` on any page.

**What that explains, and this is why it is worth writing down rather than fixing one row at a time:**

| already recorded | what it actually was |
|---|---|
| `W3627`, `W3579` - "the cast could not sign in (threw: getDb() called before @supabase/supabase-js loaded)", filed as **cold-start artifacts** | the CDN fetch losing a race, on a machine that was merely busy |
| the **offline-3g cluster** - 40% closed against 75-83% for every other condition (12 rows still open) | a 1-in-12 drop rate against a REQUIRED third-party script: lose that one request and the page has no client, no auth and no data |
| `W3512`, `W3654` - a blank `hive.html`, hops with no way onward | the same, downstream: nothing renders because nothing can read |

The offline-3g walk also unregisters the service worker, which is the correct model for a **first-time
visitor** - and a first visit is precisely the case where no cache could have helped anyway.

**RECOMMENDATION, in the order that reduces risk fastest:**

1. **Self-host the client.** Vendor `supabase.min.js` to the origin and add it to `SHELL_FILES`. That is
   the only change that makes it precacheable, removes a third-party runtime dependency from every page,
   and turns "the CDN lost a request" from a total failure into a non-event. ~37 `<script src>` edits plus
   one vendored file plus a `CACHE_NAME` bump.
2. **Until then, fail legibly.** No page carries an `onerror` on that tag, so the failure surfaces as
   `getDb() called before … loaded` thrown into the console while the person sees a blank or half-page.
   An `onerror` that shows "Couldn't load - check your connection and reload" is a few lines per page and
   turns a mystery into an instruction.
3. **Re-walk the 12 open `offline-3g` rows after (1)** and expect them to move as a group. If they do not,
   the condition is measuring the emulator rather than the platform - the falsification test this finding
   has to carry, same as the one recorded in the section above.

**Not fixed here**: (1) is a 37-page edit plus a vendored dependency and a shell-cache change, which is a
deliberate platform decision about supply chain and offline posture - Ian's call, not a walk's.

---

## W3-JN follow-through · the client is VENDORED, and the swap found a gate that could not see half the platform (2026-09-10)

**The fix from the section above is LANDED locally.** `vendor/supabase-js-2.110.0.min.js` (206,178 B) was
downloaded and proved **byte-identical to what production has been serving**: its SHA-384 is
`DjOvX/sJLsmbMrw4wTvf6l3kiGBjdxyOO6X2MTFwOOXGkjN/mE08BoDzrpaaIjil`, which is exactly the hash already pinned
in the `integrity` attribute of all 35 static tags. It is in `SHELL_FILES`, `CACHE_NAME` is at v344, and
`validate_sw_shell_membership` passes. The bundle was then loaded in a browser-shaped `vm` context and
`supabase.createClient()` built a client with working `from`/`auth`/`channel`/`functions`/`storage`/`rpc`
and a real query builder — the file works, not merely serves.

*(Three verification attempts failed before that and every one was the harness, not the file: passing
`module`/`exports` forced the UMD CommonJS branch; `new Function` makes the bundle's top-level
`var supabase` a local instead of a global; and the sandbox was missing `Headers`, then `WebSocket`.
The bundle was correct the whole time — see the standing lesson that the instrument is wrong more often
than the product.)*

### The swap's own reach was wrong — TWO paths, not one

The first sweep globbed `*.html` at the root and rewrote `<script src>` tags. That missed:

- **Five founder-gate pages** — `architecture`, `llm-observability`, `agentic-rag-observability`,
  `validator-catalog`, `symbol-gallery` — which never wrote a tag at all. They build the element in JS:
  `var s1 = document.createElement('script'); s1.src = 'https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@supabase/supabase-js@2'`
  — **floating `@2`, no `integrity` whatsoever**, the weakest contract on the platform, and it sits *inside*
  the `isPlatformAdmin()` check that decides whether the page is shown. The gate is fail-CLOSED
  (`s1.onerror = deny`), so a CDN outage denies rather than leaks; the exposure runs the other way —
  whatever `@2` resolves to tomorrow executes inside the admin check. Now vendored **and** hashed.
- **`feedback/index.html`**, one directory down, which a root-only glob never visited. It needs
  `../vendor/...`; the literal root path would have 404'd, so depth is part of the rewrite, not a detail.

### The gate that should have caught this had the right RULE and the wrong REACH

`validate_sri.py` has enforced "a version-pinned third-party script without `integrity` is a hard FAIL"
for months, and reported PASS throughout — because its reader only ever matched **tag text**, over
**root-only** files. Widened to read all four shapes a library arrives in (static tag · built in JS ·
passed to a loader helper · bound to a const and loaded elsewhere) and scoped to the pages the site
actually serves, it immediately failed on **7 real violations it had always forbidden**:

| Page | Library (all version-PINNED, all unhashed) |
|---|---|
| `integrations.html` | `pdfjs-dist@3.11.174`, `mammoth@1.6.0`, `xlsx@0.18.5` via `vehLoadScript()` |
| `resume.html` | `pdfjs-dist@3.11.174`, `mammoth@1.6.0`, `xlsx@0.18.5`, `jszip@3.10.1` via `loadScript()` |

These are the two pages that ingest a person's documents — a CV, a vehicle registration — so a compromised
jsdelivr response would have run in the page holding that document and that session. **All 7 now carry
SHA-384 hashes of the bytes jsdelivr actually serves**, threaded through the loaders exactly as this
codebase's own `loadScriptOnce` already did. Two of the six computed hashes came out **byte-identical to
hashes a previous session had independently verified and shipped**, which vouches for the other four.

**Scope is now derived, not guessed.** Root-only saw 42 pages; `rglob` then over-corrected to 551 by
sweeping `.tmp/`, `.hexvar_bak/` and Flask `templates/`, inflating the backlog to 275 refs. Vercel deploys
the git-tracked tree minus `.vercelignore`, so that is the definition the gate uses: **175 served pages**.
The older roadmap line "floating 44→9, all Tailwind" was honest about what it measured and silently wrong
about the platform; the real figures, after every hashable reference was hashed, are **0 pin-first refs** and **119 Tailwind Play-CDN pages** — plus two cross-origin workers and one provider-unpinnable Turnstile endpoint, each reported in its own bucket because no hash can cover them.

**Reported distinctly rather than folded into the FAIL count:** `pdf.worker.min.js` on both pages is a
cross-origin **worker**, fetched from a URL string with no element to carry `integrity` — SRI cannot apply,
so "add a hash" would be wrong advice and the lever is self-hosting the worker. Likewise Turnstile's
`api.js` on `index.html`, which Cloudflare serves unversioned by design.

The gate's self-test now has teeth for each reach, including an **order-reversal** case: `xlsx` is loaded
twice in `integrations.html`, once hashed and once not, so a URL's verdict is `min()` over its call sites —
deduping on first sight would certify whichever call site happened to appear first.

**The canary stays.** `browser-floor.js` still watches for a missing client, because the dependency moved
rather than vanished: the vendored file can still fail to arrive from an evicted cache or a bad deploy, and
the failure looks identical to the person.

**Still Ian's gates**: deploying this (the vendored file, the 41 changed pages, the `sw.js` bump) and the
Tailwind Play-CDN migration, which is a build-model change across 119 pages, not an SRI hash.

## Platform finding · the file that removes the prod exposure was never committed, so it never ran (measured 2026-09-10)

Found while deriving the SRI gate's scope from `.vercelignore`. `git status` reports that file as
**`?? .vercelignore` — untracked.** Vercel deploys the git tree, so an untracked ignore file is part of no
deployment and excludes nothing. It was written 2026-09-06 with a careful comment recording that the site
runs on Vercel, "which reads neither netlify.toml nor `_headers`", and that `/_fixtures/…` had been measured
at 200 on the live origin. **The intent was written down; the exposure was never removed.** Re-measured on
the live origin today, four days later:

| URL | measured now |
|---|---|
| `/_fixtures/engineering-design-test.html` | **200 · 1,729,742 B** — still fully served |
| `/test-data-seeder/templates/index.html` | **200 · 269,083 B** — the LOCAL-ONLY WorkHive Tester's Jinja template, serving raw `{{ supabase_url }}` and `{% if connected and test_logins %}` |
| `/video_marketing_app/templates/index.html` | **200 · 133,849 B** |
| `/feedback/` | 200 · 19,605 B — a real public page, and one of 18 served pages absent from the page roster |

This is [[feedback_the_config_was_for_the_wrong_platform]] running a second time at a different depth:
first a rule written into a file the platform never reads, then a rule written into the *right* file that
was never committed. From inside the repo the two are indistinguishable — a thoughtful config, no error on
save, and a false receipt for the next reader.

**Two contributing blind spots, both now closed in `validate_deploy_root_hygiene`:**

1. **The gate asserted `netlify.toml`** — the fixtures force-404 rule, its ordering against the catch-all —
   a file the deploy does not open. It now also requires `.vercelignore` to be **in HEAD** and to name every
   dev-only tree. It asks HEAD deliberately, **not the index**: `git ls-files` reports staged paths, so a
   bare `git add` would turn the check green while production stayed exposed.
2. **It swept the root only** (`ROOT.glob("*.html")`), so two dev tools' template directories were outside
   its vision entirely — the same reach defect that hid the Supabase tags, recorded in
   [[feedback_a_gates_reach_is_part_of_its_rule]].

`.vercelignore` now also excludes `test-data-seeder/`, `video_marketing_app/` and `remotion_scenes/`.

**The page roster is short by 18.** `substrate/reference/page_roster.json` holds 157 pages in three shapes
(root `*.html`, `learn/*/index.html`, `tools/*/index.html`) and `validate_page_roster` passes, because it
checks parity against those three patterns rather than against what is deployed. The served set is 175. The
missing 18 are four genuine public pages — `about/`, `feedback/`, `privacy-policy/`, `terms-of-service/` —
plus eight promo posters and the six dev templates above. `feedback/index.html` was the page still pointing
at the CDN Supabase client after the root-only swap: no instrument's definition of "the pages" contained it.

**Ian's gates**: committing `.vercelignore` (the only action that closes the three live 200s — the gate will
keep failing until it is in HEAD, by design), and deciding whether the four public pages and the promo
posters should join the roster or be declared exceptions.

## W3-JN instrument fix · a destination can have more than ONE parent, and ranking threw the others away (2026-09-10)

`prove_full_journeys.mjs` grades a hop that has no thread onward by asking whether the destination is
*parented* — reached from a specific page by design — and, since the fix recorded above it, whether the
walk had actually arrived FROM that parent. `parentedDestinations()` built that table by **ranking the
candidate linkers and keeping the single best one.** So a journey arriving via any OTHER real route was
reported as "this archetype's path skips the intended route."

Measured on this tree: **16 of 34 destinations have more than one non-index linker**; within the derived
table, **6 of 20 entries were collapsing parents.** `resume.html` is the clearest case — it is linked in
plain prose from **both** `skillmatrix.html:434` and `achievements.html:392`, which is the very fact that
justified hiding its nav entry in yesterday's nav-budget fix. The Tier-D career chains (J25+J13+J7+J31)
walk from achievements into the portfolio, a route the platform genuinely offers, and were marked **BAD**
for it: `W3715`, `W3716`, `W3717` carry that verdict and nothing else.

`PARENTED[dest]` is now the LIST of every real parent, `arrivedFromParent` asks whether the page we stood
on is among them, and the message reads "reached from A or B". `index.html` stays excluded because it links
to everything and therefore distinguishes nothing — unless it is the only linker, where it is the honest
answer. **The teeth are unchanged and proven**: arriving at `resume.html` from `skillmatrix.html` or
`achievements.html` now passes, arriving from `logbook.html` is still flagged, and a destination with no
parent at all still reports as a genuine navigation gap.

This is the same shape as the two other instrument defects found today — a rule that was correct while the
reader it depended on was too narrow ([[feedback_a_gates_reach_is_part_of_its_rule]]) — and the same
"one winner certifies the rest" arithmetic as the SRI gate's per-URL verdict, which had to become min()
over call sites.

**Re-walk queued**: Tier D is re-running behind the live J14 chain (`.tmp/rewalk_tierD_after_chain.sh`,
serial by construction — the 8 GB host runs one browser). J14 itself already picked up the fixed prover.

## §LW.2 follow-up · why this session fell back to batch tools, and the ONE fix that returns it to realtime MCPs (2026-09-10)

Ian, mid-turn: *"that is why we have to drive the roadmap in MCPs, so that we can triage it realtime, so
that we can move fast."* He is right, and this turn is the evidence. Triaging one edge-function 500 took a
dozen batch calls — `docker logs`, `curl`, process listings — and **three of them lied**:

| instrument | what it said | what was true |
|---|---|---|
| `docker logs` timestamps | "the edge container has logged nothing since yesterday 19:32" | containers run **UTC**, the host is **NZST (UTC+12)** — `19:32Z` was **07:32 today**, my own probe, minutes old |
| `curl -F "audio=@/tmp/a.mp4"` | `HTTP 000`, read as "the stack is down" | Git Bash `/tmp` writes land elsewhere, so curl had no file to attach |
| `pgrep -f "walk_archetypes\|prove_full_journeys"` | "nothing running" | **J14 was mid-walk**; Git Bash `pgrep` cannot see Windows-native processes |

That third one did real damage: a queued job took the false clear and **restarted Kong and the edge runtime
under a live walk**, and `W3700` came back "1 step(s) showed the person an error". That verdict is about my
restart, not the platform — it is queued for a re-walk rather than banked. Its replacement guard used
`wmic`, which is **not on this PATH at all** and reported "no walk detected" just as confidently. Two guards
in a row could not see the thing they guarded. The working instrument is PowerShell CIM (verified: 10
matching processes while both others said none), and the guard now treats an **unreadable answer as "a walk
IS running"** rather than as zero.

### The actual blocker for MCP-first triage, measured

The `postgres` MCP — the realtime instrument this section exists to mandate — **fails every query with
`ECONNRESET`**, and did so across a `/mcp` reconnect. Isolated:

- the DB is healthy: `docker exec … psql` returns **6 hives, 23,259 logbook rows**;
- the port publish is correct: `5432/tcp -> 0.0.0.0:54322`, SSL off, `scram-sha-256`;
- the stored credentials are correct: the **same URI password authenticates over TCP inside the container**;
- from the host, both `localhost` (which resolves to `::1`) and `127.0.0.1` fail — `server closed the
  connection unexpectedly` / timeout.

So the DB, the port map and the password are all fine, and the fault is the **Windows/WSL port-forward on
54322 dropping host connections**. `docker restart supabase_db_workhive` re-establishes the publish; it is
queued behind the running walks rather than done under them, for the reason W3700 records above. Until it is
back, DB-side triage falls to `docker exec psql`, which is a batch tool and exactly the slowness Ian named.

**RESOLVED the same turn.** `docker restart supabase_db_workhive` rebuilt the publish, and both `localhost`
and `127.0.0.1` connect again. The `postgres` MCP answered on the next call — 6 hives, 23,259 logbook rows,
23 active members, in ONE call with no `docker exec`. Its first real use confirmed something the batch tools
had made expensive to ask: **all six hives now carry the full ~1,824-day span**, so the `limit=2000` capped
read in `seed_5y_synthetic_history.py` — which had only ever seeded three of six — is fixed across every
vertical, and the month-3 / year-2 moments the Tier-C rows name are genuinely available in each.

**Standing rule this adds to §LW.2:** before falling back to a batch tool, say WHY the MCP could not answer —
and if the reason is that an MCP is down, **fixing the MCP is the higher-priority unit**, because every later
triage inherits the slowness. The whole outage was one restart; it cost a dozen batch calls and three false
readings to reach that one command. Kin: [[feedback_check_the_connected_mcps_before_declaring_a_login_ceiling]].

## W3-FN finding · SEVEN of the platform's first NINE AI models did not exist, and the gate that forbids that had never read a single model (measured 2026-09-10)

Driving the last four open W3-FN rows through the MCPs, as Ian asked. Two of the four closed on real
evidence; getting there uncovered the largest defect of the session, and it was hiding behind a sentence
that told everyone not to look.

### What was measured

Asked of each provider's own `/models` endpoint, with the platform's own working keys:

| entry in `_shared/ai-chain.ts` | provider says |
|---|---|
| `meta-llama/llama-4-scout-17b-16e-instruct` | **404 — retired** |
| `llama-3.3-70b-versatile` | **404 — retired** |
| `qwen/qwen3-32b` | **404 — retired** |
| `llama-3.1-8b-instant` | **404 — retired** |
| `openai/gpt-oss-20b` | live |
| `openai/gpt-oss-120b` | live |
| `llama-3.3-70b` (cerebras) | **404** |
| `qwen-3-32b` (cerebras) | **404** |
| `llama3.1-8b` (cerebras) | **404** |

**Every AI call on the platform spent four round-trips collecting 404s before a model answered, and the
whole Cerebras tier was decoration.** After the repair, a live call through the chain is served by the
FIRST entry in **0.45 s** — `groq / qwen/qwen3.8-27b`, verified end to end.

### Why nothing reported it

`validate_groq_fallback` has a check named "No deprecated or known-bad model IDs in the chain", with a
14-name deny-list. Its extractor searched for `"model":` — a QUOTED key — while `ai-chain.ts` is
TypeScript and writes `model:` bare. **It returned an empty list, so the check compared 14 banned names
against ZERO models, and passed, every run, for its entire life.** Measured at the moment of the fix: the
gate could see 0 while the file held 19.

A deny-list is also the wrong shape — it only ever catches a name a human remembered to add, and nobody
knew these had died. The gate now carries **`check_models_are_live`**, which ASKS each provider and fails
on any configured name it does not serve. It is network-optional (no key or no answer → it SKIPS and says
which provider it could not ask, never inventing a pass), and it is mutation-proven: 0 issues on the real
chain, 1 on a chain with one model renamed. It was also registered in `CHECK_LABELS` but not
`CHECK_NAMES` at first, so it printed a FAIL and still exited 0 — a refusal with no teeth, now fixed.

**Three copies had to move together**: `_shared/ai-chain.ts`, `tools/ai_chain.py` and
`tools/lib/ai_chain.py` — whose own header says "change one, change both" while there are three. The
`ai-chain-mirror` gate confirms all three agree at 18 models.

### `voice-model-call` — four dead models and a sentence that hid them

Its private chain named `qwen2.5-7b-instruct` (not a Cerebras model), `llama-4-scout` (retired), and —
worse — **`mistral-large-2411` at `api.voyage.ai/v1/chat/completions` and `jina-ai/reader` at
`api.jina.ai/v1/chat/completions`. Voyage and Jina are EMBEDDINGS providers; neither has ever had a chat
endpoint.** Two of its four "models" could not have worked on any day since the file was written.

It reported all of this as **"All models failed (rate limited or down)"** — a cause it had no evidence
for, because the catch that would have carried the evidence logged `{ detail: err }`, and **an `Error`
serialises to `{}`**. Every failure line this chain ever wrote read `Model qwen failed: {}`. With the
serialisation fixed, four different reasons appeared at once (404, 404, transport, 401), and not one was
a rate limit. The error path now also carries the provider's own response body — which is how the last
barrier was found, quoted verbatim: `'messages.0' : value must be an object with the discriminator
property: 'role'`.

### Four instrument defects fixed to make the claims askable at all

The prover was as wrong as the product, and its errors were being banked as platform faults:

1. **The file part was behind a string.** The multipart switch marks the part name as filled, so the
   generic filler put a STRING in `audio`; the loop appended it, then the real WAV was appended under
   the SAME name. `FormData` keeps both and the server's `form.get("audio")` returns the FIRST. The WAV
   was in the request all along.
2. **A document field got a token.** `payload` fell to the generic `'status'` fallback — six characters
   where a résumé belongs — so `resume-extract` asked a model to find jobs and skills in the word
   "status", got `{}`, and said the file was unreadable. Filed as an AI-provider ceiling; refuted by a
   falsification test (`resume-polish` answered 200 from the same chain minutes later).
3. **A number in range is not the same as a number.** `temperature` was sent as `5`; every provider
   caps it at 2.
4. **An empty array satisfies `Array.isArray` and nothing else.** A complaint naming an array was
   answered with `[]`, which passes the function's own guard, reaches the provider and is refused there.

### Rows

- **`W31238` voice-transcribe — CLOSED**, all three lenses, 0 unanswered. Its `form.get("audio") as File`
  was a cast, not a check: a non-file passed both size guards (`undefined === 0` and `undefined > 10MB`
  are both false), killed the self-host ASR with `arrayBuffer is not a function`, made every Groq model
  answer `400 missing_audio_input`, and ended in a 500 blaming the transcription providers.
- **`W31175` resume-extract — CLOSED**, all three lenses, 0 unanswered.
- **`W31229` voice-model-call** — went from "no request could ever succeed" to reaching the models; now
  429 on its own per-identity limit, which THIS probe spent. Confirming probe queued for the reset.
- **`W31154` pdf-ingest** — stays open and is NOT descoped: it is in-scope and measurably broken (nothing
  ever inserts into `pdf_jobs`; all six permitted destination tables lack the `content` and `meta`
  columns it writes). Retire-or-complete is Ian's decision, as its header says.

**Ian's gates**: deploying the repaired chain and the three edge functions. The model-name repair is a
behaviour change on every AI feature — it replaces guaranteed 404s with models the providers currently
serve, and the new gate will fail the board the day any of them is retired.

## W3-JN fixture finding · a SPAN is not a MOMENT — the three fleet hives render near-empty pages (measured 2026-09-10)

Found in one query the moment the `postgres` MCP came back, which is the point Ian was making about
driving the roadmap through the MCPs.

`validate_fixture_depth` asks whether a hive has LIVED long enough for the date a row names. Every hive
now spans ~1,824 days after the seeder repair, so every cast passes. But a row set at `month-3` renders
the hive **as it was then**, and the fleet hives hold almost nothing in those windows:

| hive | day-1 | month-3 | year-2 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Manila Electronics Assembly | — | **324** | 35 |
| Lucena Pharmaceutical Mfg. | — | **266** | 54 |
| Baguio Textile Mills | — | **200** | 44 |
| Dela Cruz Delivery Fleet | 8 | **4** | 3 |
| Ramos Jeepney Line | 5 | **1** | 5 |
| Tan Delivery Vans | 3 | **2** | 1 |

**Ramos Jeepney Line holds ONE logbook row around month-3; Tan Delivery Vans holds ONE around year-2.**
A Tier-C walk cast there measures a blank page and reports it as "the hive at month 3" — the date is
honest and the SCENE is not. The plants hold 35–324 in the same windows, so the same archetype means
something completely different depending on which vertical it is cast in.

The gate now measures **density at the moment**, not only span to it. Reported as a NOTE above zero and
FAILED at zero: how much history a small fleet should carry is a fixture decision, and a gate that fails
the board on a judgement call teaches people to ignore it — but a window with no rows means the moment
does not exist in the data at all, which no walk can render. Nine (hive, moment) pairs are currently
thin; all nine are fleet hives. Compound Tier-D moments are expanded into their parts and de-duplicated
against the standalone casts, so one shortfall is reported once rather than once per row naming it.

**For Ian**: the fleets were seeded ~10× lighter than the plants (411–611 logbook rows against
6,944–7,700). Deepening them is a seeder run, not a code change — `seed_5y_synthetic_history.py` already
knows how; it simply produced far less for the vehicle verticals. Until then, moment-cast fleet rows are
measuring a thinner platform than the archetype intends.

**FIXED the same turn, and the cause was not the history seeder.** `seed_5y_synthetic_history.py` had
worked perfectly evenly — rows-per-asset was 200–257 in every hive, plants and fleets alike. The fleets
were thin because they owned **2–3 vehicles** against the plants' 30–36, and the seeder writes 40 events
per ASSET per year. A jeepney line running two units is not a line.

`seed_fleet_history.py` already knew how to register vehicles cloned from the platform's own shape, but
its guard was `if not units` — it rescued a fleet with ZERO and did nothing for one with two. Raised to
top up to `FLEET_MIN_UNITS = 8`, skipping any plate the hive already owns, and three defects in that
change were caught before it ran: an empty VALUES list on a re-run, `units` being REPLACED rather than
extended (which would have handed every seeded job to the new vans and left the originals bare), and the
PM loop writing a duplicate schedule for every pre-existing vehicle.

**The history seeder then refused to run**, because its checkpoint asks "is every hive deep enough" and
every hive was — while 17 vehicles registered minutes earlier held nothing. That is the same shape as the
`max()` guard this file already carries a scar from: a number true about the corpus and silent about the
missing part. The checkpoint now also counts ASSETS WITHOUT HISTORY, which is the unit its own loop
iterates. Two corrections to that check before it was believed: it first joined `logbook.machine` to
`asset_nodes.name` and reported **113** unseeded assets including all 96 plant assets — impossible beside
7,000 rows per plant, because `machine` holds the TAG (`M-003`); and it counted the `enterprise`, `plant`
and `site` container nodes, which can never hold machine history and would have made the checkpoint
UNSATISFIABLE. Corrected: **20**.

The seeder's `--commit` needs `SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY`, which is not present anywhere on this machine,
so the local-substitute path was used: **7,987 rows cloned through the database** from each fleet's own
existing rows — same vocabulary, same `maintenance_type`, same `root_cause`, same workers, dates jittered
per unit — every one marked `sync_meta->>'seed' = 'fleet-unit-backfill'` and removable by that marker
alone.

| hive | month-3 before → after | year-2 before → after | logbook rows |
|---|---|---|---|
| Dela Cruz Delivery Fleet | 4 → **23** | 3 → **30** | 611 → 3,666 |
| Ramos Jeepney Line | 1 → **44** | 5 → **25** | 411 → 2,877 |
| Tan Delivery Vans | 2 → **23** | 1 → **13** | 411 → 2,877 |

`validate_fixture_depth` goes from nine thin (hive, moment) pairs to **one** — `Tan Delivery Vans` at
`day-1` with 6 rows, which is a hive's opening day and reads as realistic rather than as a gap.
